A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PETAR-4B and the same core dataset of 11,356 lesions from 5,126 exams. Their text, equations, figures and tables support comparison. V2 includes supplementary material absent from the supplied v1, despite v1 referring to supplementary details.

before.justification: V1 reports original model comparisons, component ablations and correlations between automated metrics and physician scores in Tables 3–5.

after.justification: V2 reports original model comparisons, ablations, metric correlations and physician evaluations on internal and external data in Tables 2–5, with additional analyses in its supplement.

M1.justification: The core encoding, focal cropping, feature fusion and autoregressive objective remain unchanged. Section 4.4 changes the stated alignment order from mask-then-projector to projector-then-mask and describes repeating the three-stage sequence on both training datasets. However, v2's stage headings contradict their descriptions, leaving the implemented order uncertain.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on 32 external autoPET instances, extending coverage beyond the internal PET/CT dataset. The supplement identifies an additional imaging difference: primarily contrast-enhanced CT externally versus primarily non-contrast CT internally. Renaming PETAR-11K to PETARSeg-11K does not itself change coverage.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 3, v2 Table 2 adds QoQ-Med and fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B and MedGemma-4B comparisons. The added fine-tuned 2D baselines materially strengthen comparisons under dataset adaptation. Expanded names for retained baselines are not counted as new methods.

E3.justification: The reported internal test size changes from 1,170 to 1,175, and the stated anatomical pretraining size changes from approximately 5,000 to 100,000 segmentations. V2 reports ten epochs for all stages instead of five for initial pretraining, although supplementary Table 9 still lists five. It also specifies three-view inputs for the new fine-tuned 2D comparisons and changes retained ablation rows' TS flags from enabled to disabled. These are reported setting revisions, not evidence that all experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds an explicit full-model comparison with and without TotalSegmentator pretraining, which v1's populated ablation rows did not isolate. It also adds external distribution-shift evaluation, replaces the original qualitative cases with broader baseline error comparisons in Figure 4, and supplies autoPET examples in supplementary Figure 5.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates, whereas v2 Table 5 adds plus/minus quantities to physician ratings. Their statistical meaning is not specified. Neither version reports training-run uncertainty, seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: PETAR's reported BLEU, CIDEr and GREEN change from 0.531, 0.415 and 0.246 to 0.535, 0.457 and 0.257; changed settings prevent interpreting these as controlled performance gains. GREEN's human correlation changes from 0.608 to 0.592, and other metric correlations and rankings change. V2 additionally reports new comparator results, internal physician scores and preference counts (15 preferred, 54 tied, 47 not preferred), external ratings and cohort statistics.

T1.justification: The cropping, encoding, fusion and likelihood equations retain their mathematical substance. V2 makes mask embeddings and notation more explicit and numbers more equations, but introduces no substantive theoretical result, proof or changed formal assumption.

C1.justification: The central dataset, mask-aware model and improved findings-generation claims remain. V2 adds an explicit novelty claim in the abstract that its five-physician evaluation is the first human study of automated PET reporting.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly acknowledges hallucinated numerical measurements and qualifies the reader evaluation by explaining their exclusion. It also discusses PET domain shift, possible overrating by automated metrics and external generalization. Dependence on supplied masks and a future fully automated reporting pipeline were already discussed in v1.

D1.justification: V2's supplement supplies acquisition and deidentification details, the formatting prompt, software libraries, LoRA placement, precision, batch size, learning rate and other hyperparameters. It also documents reader blinding, numerical masking, viewing software and scoring rubrics. These are substantial new disclosures, although conflicting epoch counts and training descriptions limit reproducibility.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands citations supporting baseline models, PET datasets, evaluation metrics, implementation tools and segmentation workflows. It sharpens the distinction from Reg2RG's organ-level, single-modality setting and develops the relationship to Describe Anything's focal prompting; Describe Anything was already cited in v1.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, results and explanatory passages. It reorganizes experimental setup and human evaluation, replaces the standalone PETAR-Bench and Discussion sections with revised setup and limitations sections, renames the dataset, and adds a structured supplement.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are substantially redrawn, and Figure 4 becomes a larger comparison matrix with anatomical error annotations. V2 removes the model-capability table, redesigns the dataset comparison table, reorganizes experimental tables and adds physician-results and supplementary displays. These changes extend well beyond numerical updates and renumbering.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves a major evidential gap by publishing quantitative physician outcomes that v1's clinical-utility claims lacked, adding a limited external evaluation and testing fine-tuned 2D competitors. Its supplement materially improves methodological transparency, including disclosure that numerical hallucinations were excluded from reader scoring. Conflicting training-stage descriptions, epoch counts and some prose/table values remain, but the strengthened clinical evidence and documentation provide a substantial net improvement.
